Did the Iran war throw the world into chaos? Sadegh Alhosseini

From February 28 to today, gasoline has gotten more expensive in 145 countries. 29 countries have seen serious street protests. Paris made 1,800 arrests in a single day, Bolivia saw 17 killed, and in Tirana government buildings went up in flames.

So the short answer is: yes, the shock of this war reached the entire world.

But the chart says something else too — something more important.

Point one: Nigeria had a 75 percent fuel price hike and stayed calm. Albania had 17 percent and went up in flames.

Point two: America saw a 52 percent increase and its protesters committed almost no violence, yet Trump is losing Congress. And France, at 33 percent, saw looting and arson.

Point three: The Iran war is driving political change in various countries. It's only the cost you impose on the world that makes a war end in your victory — not any kind of international law!

@sadegh_alhosseini

entry.title: [sadegh_alhosseini] If someone says "I'll make you a billionaire overnight," we don't need to ask…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @sadegh_alhosseini

If someone says "I'll make you a billionaire overnight," we don't need to ask for the details to know it's a pipe dream. "Zero inflation" amid 90% inflation is the same story. The municipality spokesman says Al-Hosseini doesn't know the details. True — the city council member doesn't know either, and says they found out from the media. But one question is enough: where does the money come from? There are only three ways: 1. Fixed-rate currency from the Central Bank: the gap gets covered by printing money — meaning inflation for all of Iran. 2. Zero-percent loans and buying now: the bank's loss ultimately gets covered by creating money — the same as the first way. 3. Municipality budget: no budget has been approved, and if it were, it's the money for Tehranis' own metro and buses. Either the plan falls short midway, or someone else pays for it. It's not zero inflation; it's inflation that's been sent somewhere else.@sadegh_alhosseini

entry.title: [sadegh_alhosseini] US inflation hit 3.7 percent in September — higher than economists' forecast…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @sadegh_alhosseini

US inflation hit 3.7 percent in September — higher than economists' forecast of 3.6 percent and the highest figure since May. Before the Esfand war, US inflation stood at 2.4 percent, and experts had projected just 2.6 percent for all of 2026. With the closure of Hormuz, US gasoline prices jumped 21 percent in a single month, and inflation reached 4.2 percent within three months. A seventy-year comparison shows that war alone doesn't rattle US inflation: The Afghanistan war: forecasts remained almost unchanged. The Iraq war: inflation came in 14 percent lower than forecast. The Ukraine war: inflation came in 71 percent higher than forecast. The Iran war: so far 42 percent higher than forecast. What sets the Iran war apart from the Iraq and Afghanistan wars is this: it is directly wired to Americans' gas pumps. Every month Hormuz stays closed widens this gap, and that is why America must exit this war as soon as possible.@sadegh_alhosseini
